Series::aminmax¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

std::pair<Series, Series> Series::aminmax() const
std::pair<Series, Series> Series::aminmax(std::int64_t dim, bool keepdim = false) const

What It Does¶

Returns the smallest and the largest value together, as one call.

aminmax() exists because “what is the range of this data” is a single question, and answering it by calling amin() and amax() separately walks the tensor twice and reads as two unrelated statements. aminmax() walks it once and hands back a std::pair<Series, Series> — .first is the minimum, .second is the maximum — so the pair travels together into whatever needs both: an axis range for a plot, the denominator of a min-max rescale, a sanity-check bound, the endpoints for histogram().

Two forms:

  • aminmax() collapses the whole tensor to two scalars.

  • aminmax(dim, keepdim) reduces one axis. Each result has the input shape with dim removed, or kept as a length-1 axis when keepdim is true.

The order in the pair is always (min, max).

Parameters¶

dim (std::int64_t): the axis to reduce. Negative values count from the end. Omit it (call the no-argument form) to reduce every axis.

keepdim (bool): when true, the reduced axis stays in the result as a length-1 dimension so the outputs still broadcast against the input. Default false.

Returns¶

std::pair<Series, Series> {min, max}. Both pieces share the input’s dtype and platform. The whole-tensor form yields two 0-D scalars; the dim form yields two series shaped like the input with dim reduced.

Structured bindings read cleanly: auto [lo, hi] = x.aminmax();.

Gradient¶

Both channels are differentiable. In a reverse pass:

  • the gradient arriving at .first (the min) is routed to the input position that held the minimum,

  • the gradient arriving at .second (the max) is routed to the position that held the maximum,

  • every other position receives 0.

If several positions tie for the extremum, the incoming gradient is split evenly among them (the same rule amin() / amax() use). Integer inputs carry no gradient.

Examples¶

Example 1. The whole-tensor form: two scalars.

auto [lo, hi] =
    pluss::make_series({3.0, 1.0, 4.0, 1.0, 5.0, 9.0, 2.0, 6.0}).aminmax();

std::cout << "min=" << lo;
std::cout << "max=" << hi;

Output¶

min=pluss::Series(shape=[], strides=[], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=1max=pluss::Series(shape=[], strides=[], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=9

Example 2. dim = 0 reduces down each column; the axis is dropped.

auto m = pluss::make_series({
    {1.0, 5.0, 2.0},
    {8.0, 3.0, 7.0},
    {4.0, 0.0, 9.0},
});
auto [lo, hi] = m.aminmax(0);

std::cout << "min=" << lo;
std::cout << "max=" << hi;

Output¶

min=pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[1, 0, 2]max=pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[8, 5, 9]

Column 0 ranges 1..8, column 1 ranges 0..5, column 2 ranges 2..9.

Example 3. keepdim = true keeps the reduced axis as length 1, so the results still line up against the input for broadcasting.

auto m = pluss::make_series({{1.0, 5.0, 2.0}, {8.0, 3.0, 7.0}});
auto [lo, hi] = m.aminmax(1, true);

std::cout << "min=" << lo;
std::cout << "max=" << hi;

Output¶

min=pluss::Series(shape=[2,1], strides=[1,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[[1],
  [3]]max=pluss::Series(shape=[2,1], strides=[1,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[[5],
  [8]]

Example 4. Because the pair travels together, the span is one subtraction.

auto [lo, hi] =
    pluss::make_series({{2.0, 9.0, 4.0}, {6.0, 1.0, 8.0}}).aminmax(1);

pluss::series::print(std::cout, hi.sub(lo));

Output¶

Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[7.0000, 7.0000]

Both rows happen to span exactly 7.

Example 5. NaN propagates: a single NaN anywhere in a reduced group makes both the min and the max NaN for that group.

auto [lo, hi] = pluss::make_series(
    {1.0, std::numeric_limits<double>::quiet_NaN(), 3.0}).aminmax();

std::cout << "min=" << lo;
std::cout << "max=" << hi;

Output¶

min=pluss::Series(shape=[], strides=[], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=nanmax=pluss::Series(shape=[], strides=[], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=nan

This matches amin() / amax() and the wider reduction convention — an unknown value makes the extremes unknown. To get the extremes of the finite values only, drop the NaNs first (for example x.index_select(0, x.isnan().logical_not().nonzero().squeeze(-1))) or use a NaN-aware statistic.

Example 6. Both channels are differentiable, each routing its gradient to the position of its extremum. Here min = 1 is tied between positions 1 and 3.

auto x = pluss::make_series({3.0, 1.0, 4.0, 1.0, 5.0});
x.tracks_slope_(true);

auto [lo, hi] = x.aminmax();
(lo.mul(10.0).add(hi.mul(100.0))).reverse();

pluss::series::print(std::cout, x.sensitivity());

Output¶

Series(shape=[5], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=5, contiguous=true)
data=[0.0000, 5.0000, 0.0000, 5.0000, 100.0000]

The 100 weight on max lands entirely on position 4 (the value 5). The 10 weight on min is split between the two tied 1s, 5 each.

Example 7. Reducing an empty tensor is an error — there is no minimum or maximum to report.

try {
  auto range = pluss::series::zeros({0}).aminmax();
  (void)range;
} catch (const std::exception& e) {
  std::string msg = e.what();
  std::cout << msg.substr(0, msg.find('\n'));
}

Output¶

aminmax: cannot reduce over an empty tensor

Example 8. Negative dim counts from the end.

auto [lo, hi] = pluss::make_series({{1.0, 5.0}, {8.0, 3.0}}).aminmax(-1);

std::cout << "min=" << lo;
std::cout << "max=" << hi;

Output¶

min=pluss::Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[1, 3]max=pluss::Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[5, 8]

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • The pair is (min, max), in that order. auto [lo, hi] is the natural binding; auto [hi, lo] compiles and silently swaps the meaning.

  • NaN propagates: any NaN in a reduced group makes both outputs NaN for that group. Filter NaN first if you want the finite extremes.

  • Reducing an empty tensor, or an empty dim, raises.

  • There is no keepdim on the whole-tensor form — it always produces 0-D scalars.

  • Complex inputs have no ordering and are rejected.

  • Both outputs carry gradient; do not assume aminmax() is a detached read-only summary.

Summary¶

aminmax() is the minimum and maximum in a single reduction:

  • returns std::pair<Series, Series> = {min, max} — bind as auto [lo, hi] = ...

  • whole-tensor form gives two scalars; aminmax(dim, keepdim) reduces one axis

  • NaN propagates (matches amin / amax)

  • both channels differentiable; gradient routes to the extremum position, ties shared

  • empty input raises

See Also¶

  • Series::amin / Series::amax: the two halves on their own, when you only need one.

  • Series::max / Series::min: the value/index pair form (max_pair / min_pair) when you also want where the extremum is.

  • Series::histogram: a common consumer — aminmax() gives the default bin range.

  • Series::clamp_min / Series::clamp_max: apply a bound rather than measure one.
